clue.text: Pay out is correct

blocks.note: first meaning: to take revenge on, make someone suffer for something
second meaning: as a verb, to discipline or chastise

explanation.surface: Someone insists that handing over the money is the right thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pay out' looks like spending money and 'correct' like an adjective; both are verbs for inflicting a penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay someone out is to get even with them, and to correct a child is to discipline them; both mean inflict a penalty.

clue.text: Just deserts for those named, presumably

definitions.text: Just deserts for those named, presumably

blocks.clueFragment: Just deserts for those named, presumably
blocks.note: surface reading: the proper reward for people who have been identified

blocks.clueFragment: Just deserts for those named, presumably
blocks.note: setter's reading: an old army saying promises that nobody unnamed can be punished, so a soldier who is named gets a punishment of marching in full kit

explanation.surface: Whoever gets named will presumably get what they deserve.
explanation.walkthrough: The British saying 'no names, no pack drill' means nobody can be punished if nobody is named; turn it around and the named get the drill.
explanation.definitionFit: Pack drill was a military punishment of marching in full kit, the deserved penalty for an offending soldier.

clue.text: Skittle is new., in knotty pine

indicators.note: knotty wood is twisted and tangled, so these letters come out tangled too

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A skittle has been newly carved from a piece of knotty pine.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed punctuation after 'new' is a scanning blemish; read it as 'new, in knotty pine', all three words going into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninepin is one of the pins knocked down in the old game of skittles, so it is a skittle.

clue.text: Lace others' gins after shaking

indicators.note: a cocktail is mixed by shaking it, so these letters are stirred up into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone spikes other people's gin drinks after mixing them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lace' reads as a verb meaning to spike a drink; it is the noun for what ties a shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoe-string is the cord threaded through eyelets to fasten a shoe, which is exactly what a lace is.

clue.text: False incentives to hold debtor's note

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one word wraps around the other

blocks.note: spurs urge a horse on, so they are incentives
an IOU is the note a debtor writes, 'I owe you'

explanation.surface: Offering bonuses to make someone keep a debt note is a dodgy business.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurious means not genuine or counterfeit, a direct synonym for false.

clue.text: She, for example, goes to church to make solemn statement

indicators.note: going to a place means arriving next to it, so one piece is followed by the next

blocks.note: she is an example of a pronoun
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A woman attends church in order to make a solemn vow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' seems to be a woman going to church; it is just a word, an example of a part of speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To pronounce is to declare formally, as a judge pronounces sentence, which is making a solemn statement.

clue.text: Liturgy sounds appropriate

indicators.note: something that sounds like a word is heard, not seen, so we go by how it is said

blocks.note: right means fitting or appropriate

explanation.surface: The order of service seems fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite is a prescribed religious ceremony, and a liturgy is the set form of public worship.

clue.text: Sadly for musicians, not opening the sherry

indicators.note: without its opening means the first letter is taken away

blocks.note: doloroso is the Italian performance direction meaning sorrowfully

explanation.surface: Sadly the musicians are not opening the sherry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' looks like comment on the band's bad luck; with 'for musicians' it is a score marking.
explanation.definitionFit: Oloroso is a dark, rich style of Spanish sherry from Jerez.

clue.text: Woodland deity for a year— and a day over

indicators.note: in a down answer, over means placed above, so this piece comes first

blocks.note: Sat is the abbreviation for Saturday, a day
YR is the abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A forest god is worshipped for a year and a day beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: A satyr is a half-goat, half-man spirit of the woods in Greek mythology.

clue.text: Easy pace of David Copperfield

blocks.note: first meaning: a gait between walking and running
second meaning: the nickname Aunt Betsey gives David in Dickens's novel

explanation.surface: Dickens's hero strolls along at a leisurely pace.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's David Copperfield, Betsey Trotwood calls her great-nephew by a short form of her own surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A trot is a jogging gait, and Trot is the pet name David is given by his aunt in the novel.

clue.text: Profile of county's opener, playing overseas?

indicators.note: an opener is what comes first, so only the initial letter is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of county
a team playing abroad is on tour

explanation.surface: A cricket writer profiles the county's opening batsman while the team plays abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener' suggests an opening batsman in a county cricket team; it simply takes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A contour is an outline of a shape, and a profile is an outline seen from the side.

clue.text: Unacceptable standard in distant settlement

blocks.note: out means not allowed, as in 'that's out'
a standard is an upright pole or support

explanation.surface: Living conditions in a remote colony fall below an acceptable level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' reads as a level of quality; here it is an upright pole.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpost is a small settlement or station far from the main centres of population.

clue.text: Declaration of how things stood at Camptown?

blocks.note: the song 'Camptown Races' writes 'the' in dialect, 'De Camptown ladies sing this song'
the position is how things stand

explanation.surface: A statement explaining the state of affairs at a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Foster's minstrel song 'Camptown Races' spells 'the' as 'de', so the Camptown version of 'the position' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A deposition is a sworn written statement of evidence, a formal declaration made for a court.

clue.text: Playback of Othello, say

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: split into play, meaning room to move as in a rope with some play in it, then back

explanation.surface: Someone listens to a recording of Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playback' looks like one word about recordings; split it into 'play' and 'back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello, Shakespeare's general of Venice, is a North African, and 'say' marks him as one example.

clue.text: Carton-preserved type — one of the best

blocks.note: first meaning: Sydney Carton in A Tale of Two Cities goes to the guillotine to save Charles Darnay, a French nobleman
second meaning: from the Greek for rule by the best people

explanation.surface: A sort of thing kept in a cardboard box is first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carton' looks like a box for preserving goods; it is Sydney Carton, hero of Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities.
explanation.definitionFit: Darnay is a French noble saved by Carton, and the Greek aristos means best, so nobles are literally the best.

clue.text: Works in a road, surrounded by pubs

indicators.note: what is surrounded sits inside, so these letters go within the outer word

blocks.note: inns are pubs
taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: There are roadworks going on in a street lined with pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Works' reads as roadworks in the street; it means the inner workings of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Innards are the internal parts of a machine, the same as its works or mechanism.

clue.text: Hard job to make a rudder-holder

blocks.note: stern means hard or severe
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: Making a rudder mount is difficult work.
explanation.definitionFit: The sternpost is the upright timber at a ship's stern on which the rudder is hung.

clue.text: Sort of jacket for terrier

definitions.note: the answer is the breed name, used like an adjective before terrier

blocks.note: first meaning: a belted tweed jacket with box pleats
second meaning: a small, short-legged breed of terrier

explanation.surface: Someone buys a particular style of coat for their little dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the jacket and the terrier are named after an English county on the east coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The belted tweed country coat and a small red working dog breed both carry the name of this East Anglian county.

clue.text: Sovereign-stamper in Warwick, for example

blocks.note: first meaning: whimsically, one who makes a sovereign, read as one who makes a monarch rather than strikes a gold coin
second meaning: the Earl of Warwick, nicknamed for making and unmaking kings in the Wars of the Roses

explanation.surface: A coin minter works in the town of Warwick.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is an old British gold coin, so 'sovereign-stamper' sounds like a mint; but a sovereign is also a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, put Edward IV and then Henry VI on the throne, earning him the famous nickname.

clue.text: Bony plates of retiring oriental creature

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: E is east, the oriental direction
an animal is a creature

explanation.surface: The armour of a shy creature from the East is made of bony plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Laminae are thin layers or plates, a term used in anatomy for flat bony plates such as parts of a vertebra.

clue.text: Tinker takes in a stray

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a tinker mends pots and pans
taken as written

explanation.surface: A travelling tinker gives shelter to a stray animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' looks like a lost animal being taken in; it is a verb meaning to wander.
explanation.definitionFit: To meander is to wander aimlessly, and to stray is to wander from the proper path.

clue.text: Letter from overseas is left open, carelessly

indicators.note: doing things carelessly leaves them in a mess, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: A letter posted from abroad has been left unsealed through carelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter from overseas' looks like airmail; it is a character of a foreign alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth character of the Greek alphabet, so it is a letter from abroad.

clue.text: Soft element of endless humility, it turns out

indicators.note: with no end means the final letter is cut off
turning out suggests things coming out differently, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Gentleness is part of boundless modesty, so it emerges.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithium is a chemical element, a soft silvery metal that can be cut with a knife.

clue.text: Fish daily

blocks.note: first meaning: a trout-like freshwater fish
second meaning: a cleaning woman, also called a daily

explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like an adverb about eating fish; in Britain a daily is a cleaner who comes in each day.
explanation.definitionFit: The char is a fish related to trout, and a char or charwoman is a British cleaning lady.

clue.text: Confess with firm expression of disgust

blocks.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a firm
ugh is what you say in disgust

explanation.surface: A suspect admits guilt with an expression of disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: To cough is British police slang for owning up to a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: In criminal slang, to cough means to own up or admit guilt, so it means confess.

clue.text: Before the departure of Julius Caesar, for example

definitions.text: Before the departure of Julius Caesar, for example

blocks.note: ante is Latin for before
death, the final departure, in the Latin a Roman would use
no letters: a Roman, signalling that both pieces are read in Latin

explanation.surface: Something happens just before the Roman leader sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Departure' is a euphemism for death, and Caesar is there to signal that the answer is Latin: ante plus mortem.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means prior to death, used of events or examinations made while a person is still alive.

clue.text: Tailless antelope in dash

indicators.note: without a tail means the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: an eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: An antelope that has lost its tail is running at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dash' looks like a sprint; it means flair and style.
explanation.definitionFit: Elan is vigour and style, and dash is spirited flair, as in cutting a dash.

clue.text: A clear desert

definitions.note: used as an adjective, as in desert land

blocks.note: taken as written
to rid is to clear, as in ridding a house of mice

explanation.surface: A wide, empty wasteland of sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' and 'desert' look like adjective and noun; clear is a verb and desert describes dry land.
explanation.definitionFit: Arid means very dry and barren, the defining quality of desert land.

clue.text: Weather less than fair, say

blocks.note: under means less than, as in under ten
a fair go is a fair chance, so a go is a turn, of which a fair one is an example

explanation.surface: A forecast calls the weather a bit worse than fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weather' looks like rain or shine; it is a verb, as in weathering a storm.
explanation.definitionFit: To weather a hardship is to come through it, and to undergo something is to experience or endure it.

clue.text: Not well up?

blocks.note: surface reading: not well informed, not knowledgeable about a subject
setter's reading: feeling unwell while up in the sky in an aeroplane

explanation.walkthrough: 'Well up' is an idiom for knowledgeable; read 'up' as aloft and 'well' as healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer describes nausea caused by the motion of flying, which is being ill while high above the ground.

clue.text: Genetics evolving third eye?

indicators.note: something evolving develops into a new form, so these letters change their arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Could a third eye arise through genetic evolution?
explanation.definitionFit: Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring, the subject studied by genetics.

clue.text: Common cheat appears in costume regalia

indicators.note: something that appears in a phrase is found inside it, spanning the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A cheap swindle shows up in a fancy-dress set of royal finery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Common' marks the answer as slang, not as a description of the cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: Stumer is British slang for a forgery or a dud cheque, so it is a sham, and 'common' flags it as vulgar usage.
